Two months ago, I publicly published an Android app called "grab am" (now just "grab") designed to make it easy to download videos from social media platforms like Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, and YouTube. The idea came to me as I started to become more impatient with the typical ad-infested online tools that usually took up to five minutes or more to download a single video. So I thought to myself one day: "What if I simply built an app that could do this without the ad problem, and on top of that, wouldn't require me to copy a link, minimise the app, open a separate downloader, paste the link, and then tap download?" And thus was grab born. To download a video with grab, all you need do is tap the share button on the video and share it to grab. The download starts immediately without you ever having to leave the social media app you’re using. You simply share the video to grab and continue scrolling.
However, about two weeks ago, grab ran into a series of highly intractable problems that were so severe that, after spending about 14 hours trying to resolve them with very little progress, I started to really think the app had perhaps seen its best days. The problems incapacitated the app from downloading videos from every aforementioned social platform except Twitter.
 The Original Plan: Three Ways to Download
When I first conceived of grab, one of the first things I did was to check whether similar apps already existed—they did (obviously). With grab, though, I wanted to offer three primary ways of downloading a video: 1) using a quick settings tile, whereby you copy a video link, pull down your quick settings panel, tap the grab tile, and the video starts downloading. 2) using the share menu, whereby you simply share a video to grab and it starts downloading. 3) pasting directly into the app—you open grab and paste your video link.
I took this specific idea to Claude AI, and it told me that apps like this already existed, but the Quick Settings tile idea had never been implemented. Wanting to do something novel, I was motivated to go ahead and build grab (but little did I know I was about to fall into a bottomless pit). I then asked the AI if it had other “quick-download” ideas for the app. It mentioned a couple of ideas that sounded good on paper but were actually unimplementable in practice, the most outstanding of them being a feature whereby, immediately after you copied a social media video link, the app would detect it and send you a notification asking whether you wanted to download the video. If you tapped “Yes”, the video would immediately start downloading—all without opening grab or leaving the social media app you were using.
 Android Said "No"
I went into work, and after spending well over 25 grueling hours trying to implement these never-before-done features, especially the Quick Settings tile, I soon began to understand why they had never been done before. I quipped about it to myself: “Did you really think you were the first person to have thought about this magnificent idea? Lmao. Obviously there is a reason why no developer has yet done it.” I won’t go into all the technical details of why these radical ideas couldn’t be implemented, except to say that the Android OS, starting with Android 10, fundamentally locked down background access to the clipboard. An app can no longer see what you copy unless it is actively open on your screen or has what is called “window focus”. Because all these features relied on background services trying to access the video link you just copied without triggering an active foreground service, they were immediately killed by the OS. There are workarounds, but none of them work reliably—they lead to either a clunky user experience or a bunch of unpredictable behaviours that aren't worth the value they provide.
Only the share-menu approach works, and that's because it plays by Android's rules. When you use the share menu, the social media app packages the video link into a system message (called an "Intent" in Android development) and hands it directly to grab. Because the link is handed over rather than copied, grab never needs to look at your clipboard, thereby completely bypassing the strict clipboard privacy restrictions that killed the background-listening ideas. Thus, my original three-way download method was slashed to two efficient ways. grab was launched and the APK hosted on a simple Cloudflare website for others (mainly my WhatsApp contacts) to download and use. But like I earlier remarked, the poor app soon faced problems that almost wiped it out of its short-lived existence.
 When Everything Broke
It would probably be best to start with a general overview of how grab works. We can divide grab into two major parts: the Android part and the backend part. The Android part is the part you interact with: the part where you paste a link and tap “download”, the part that appears in your share menu, the part that sends you notifications/toast messages such as “Extracting video…” and “Download complete”. Basically, it’s the part I’ve been talking about this whole time. The backend part is where the video extraction logic lives. It isn’t part of the Android app itself, but instead, lives on an external remote server that communicates with the Android app. The Android is written in Kotlin, while the backend is written in Python.
When you tap to download a video, a summary of 5 things happen:
The Android part sends the video link to the backend part, an extraction engine, which lives on a remote server/computer.The server receives the link and uses the Python code I gave it to extract the video therein. To do this, the code: a) first tries to quickly pass the link to a fast, third-party extraction API called Cobalt. If Cobalt fails, then: b) it falls back to my own custom, heavily modified extraction engine powered by a tool called yt-dlp. Assuming one of those works:The extracted video is then transported over the internet back to the Android app.As grab receives the data, it hands it off to the native Android Download Manager, which then downloads the video and saves it to your phone’s local storage (your gallery).When Android’s Download Manager finishes writing the file to your phone, grab catches the success signal, fires off a friendly “Download complete” toast message, and you can instantly watch or share the video.Simple and straightforward, right? Well, “not so fast”, says YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram.
 Bringing grab Back to Life
Here is a summary of the major hurdles I had to overcome later to get grab actually working.
Bot detection. Somewhere around Step 2 above, social media platforms typically try to verify that the “thing” attempting to retrieve a video from their servers is actually a human being and not a bot. And because the thing in this case is a datacenter server (Render/Hugging Face) with an IP address that these platforms have generally blacklisted, they immediately block the extraction from taking place (YouTube is the strictest about this). This is where Cobalt comes in. Cobalt is a free, open-source web application designed to extract videos from major internet platforms. It is maintained by a bunch of developers and has been designed to bypass these bot checks. When I first launched grab, I simply handed the extraction work over to one of Cobalt’s public APIs. Recently, however, the developers of Cobalt closed that door and began requiring an API key to use their service. According to Gemini, I could apparently get one for free simply by asking the developers. I decided to keep that as my last option and instead tried to build my own bot-detection bypass system. Let’s just say I saw HELL, but by making use of yt-dlp, cookies, Proof-of-Origin tokens, and other elegant plugins and mechanisms, I was eventually able to bypass YouTube’s bot-detection system and successfully extract videos.After crossing that hurdle, I noticed that Instagram and Facebook videos would sometimes download without sound—or sometimes with sound but no video. They were also downloading in formats such as AV1 and HEVC that weren’t uploadable to WhatsApp or other media platforms. This hadn’t happened before, so what changed? What I didn’t realise was that Cobalt used to help me convert those video formats into a universally playable format. It also helped merge the separate video and audio streams into a single stream during the extraction process. Well, I no longer had access to their API. Which meant that, in addition to the bot-detection problem I had just spent more than 10 hours solving, I now had another problem that would probably take another six hours to solve. And solve it I did. First, I used a tool called FFmpeg to merge the video and audio streams into a single file. That part wasn’t too difficult. But converting the video formats into WhatsApp-compatible media was where I truly understood that “khaki no be leather.” More on that in the next point.grab’s backend was initially hosted on Hugging Face, which has a very generous free tier offering 16 GB of RAM and 2 vCPUs. However, Hugging Face servers aren’t optimised for web services and APIs, and they explicitly prohibit using their servers, which are primarily designed to host machine-learning programmes, as web proxies. So I had to move the backend to Render, which offers only 512 MB of RAM and 0.1 vCPU on its free tier. Now, because I no longer depend on Cobalt, the server has to directly do all the work of bypassing YouTube’s bot checks, merging separate video and audio streams, and, to solve the unsupported-media problem, transcoding HEVC codecs into universally compatible H.264 codecs. These were just very gigantic and impossible tasks to carry out on Render. Thankfully, it turns out that social media platforms actually store multiple versions of the same video in different formats on their servers. And so all I had to do was engineer a highly specific format-selection query that would forcefully ignore the HEVC/AV1 formats and return only the universally compatible H.264 video streams and AAC audio streams. I also put together a series of other improvisations to better manage the tiny amount of RAM I was allocated. At the end of the day, grab was fully back to life.It would be an understatement to say I spent a cumulative of 25 hours working on these issues. Indeed I almost gave up. There were also other minor issues on the Android/frontend side, as well as the very real “human” issue of trying not to get carried away watching reels while testing the app. But I am glad my efforts paid off.
To be sure, the grab app is by no means 100% infallible to future problems. There is a reason services like Cobalt and yt-dlp have multiple developers working on them every day to keep them robust: social media platforms are constantly changing and tightening their defences. Sometimes, keeping grab working is as simple as rotating an expired cookie or updating a dependency. Other times, I have to do absolutely insane amounts of work just for the app to continue working. After what I've been through, I can't promise myself I would be able to go through such a rigorous exercise again.
Anyway, to get the new and working version of grab, visit: grabsocialvideos.vercel.app
For those who have the old version, make sure to uninstall and delete the old APK first. And after you’ve installed the new APK, you can go ahead and delete the downloaded APK file. You don’t need it for the app to work.
 Few Tips:

A video may fail to download on the first try (due to server cold starts). Retry it immediately and it should work.Downloading from Twitter using the share menu is a bit buggy. Don't scroll right away after sharing—wait until the download has progressed significantly.Alright, bye, and see you guys next time.(Jesus, my neck hurts from writing.)#android #kotlin #python #opensource #software #coding #development #engineering #inclusive #communityBuilding an Android Social-Media-Video-Downloader App Was Much Harder Than I Expected

I've been learning Python by building a video clipping CLI application, and along the way I've ended up learning a lot more than I expected.
Some of it was straightforward. Some of it made me stop and think, especially when I first started writing tests.
Things like:
How does pytest even know which functions are tests?Why does everyone keep putting things in conftest.py?When should I use a fixture?What's the difference between patch and monkeypatch?Why did my mock not work when I was sure I patched the right thing?When should I mock something, and when should I just run the real thing?What's the point of parametrization when I could just use a loop?How do I debug one failing test without running the entire suite every time?These are the kinds of things that can feel like arbitrary rules when you're first encountering them.
Once I understood the reasoning behind them, though, pytest started making a lot more sense.
So this isn't meant to be a complete pytest reference or an explanation of every feature pytest has. It's more like a collection of the things that finally "clicked" for me while testing a real Python project.
The examples are based on my video clipping CLI, so you'll see things like FFmpeg, video metadata, audio extraction, transcription, temporary files, external dependencies, and slow tests.
Hopefully, if you're also learning Python by building something rather than just following tutorials, some of these lessons save you a few of the "why does it work like that?" moments I had. 
 Installing pytest
If you're using uv, installing pytest and coverage support is straightforward:
uv add --dev pytest pytest-covuv run pytest --version
You now have everything needed to start writing and running tests.
 Your First Test
A pytest test can be nothing more than a function:
# tests/core/test_video_inspector.py
from clipper.core.video_inspector import get_video_metadata
def test_get_video_metadata_returns_none_on_missing_file(): result = get_video_metadata("does_not_exist.mp4") assert result is None
Run it with:
uv run pytest
That's it.
There is no base class, no registration, and no decorator required.
pytest finds the test because:
the file starts with test_the function starts with test_That naming convention is the mechanism.
 How Does pytest Find Your Tests?
pytest automatically walks the current directory and its subdirectories looking for test files.
By default, it looks for files matching patterns such as:
test_*.py*_test.py
Inside those files, it looks for functions matching:
test_*
and, inside classes whose names start with Test*, methods that also match test_*.
So this:
tests/└── core/ └── test_video_inspector.py
is enough for pytest to discover the file automatically. You don't need to register the test anywhere.
This is also why commands such as:
uv run pytest --cov=src
work without explicitly listing every test file. pytest's discovery mechanism does the work.
 Assertions: Just Use assert
One of the nicest things about pytest is that you use Python's built-in assert.
def test_fps_math(): assert round(29.970029970029969, 2) == 29.97
You don't need a collection of methods like:
assertEqual(...)assertTrue(...)assertFalse(...)assertIn(...)
Instead, pytest rewrites assert statements when running tests so that failures contain useful information about what each side evaluated to. That makes a failed assertion much more informative than simply:
Assertion failed
 Comparing Floats with pytest.approx
Don't compare floating-point calculations using exact equality.
Instead:
import pytest
def test_duration_seconds(): assert 125.5 == pytest.approx(float("125.500001"))
Floating-point calculations rarely land exactly where you expect. This matters especially when dealing with things like frame rates, durations, timestamps, or calculations involving Fraction.
Without pytest.approx, you might end up writing this everywhere:
assert abs(actual - expected) < 0.001
pytest.approx gives you the tolerance without repeating that boilerplate.
pytest.approx Works with Nested Structures
pytest.approx isn't limited to individual numbers. You can use it when comparing nested structures:
def test_transcribe_matches_golden_output( sample_speech_path, sample_transcript,): result = transcribe(str(sample_speech_path))
 assert result == pytest.approx(sample_transcript)
This is particularly useful for regression or "golden file" tests. Imagine a transcript like:
{ "segments": [ { "start": 0.123456, "end": 1.987654, "words": [ {"word": "hello", "start": 0.123}, {"word": "world", "start": 0.456}, ], } ]}
You don't want to write a loop comparing every timestamp manually. pytest.approx can recursively compare numeric values with tolerance while still using normal equality for strings and other values — so it's practical to compare an entire expected transcript while allowing for harmless floating-point differences.
 Testing That an Error Is Actually Raised
When the expected behavior is for a function to raise an exception, use pytest.raises.
import pytest
def test_extract_audio_raises_on_bad_codec(): with pytest.raises(ffmpeg.Error): extract_audio( "in.mp4", "out.wav", codec="not_a_real_codec", )
This test verifies two things:
The code raises an exception.The exception is the expected type.The test fails if the function doesn't raise anything. It also fails if it raises a different exception type. Both outcomes are useful information.
pytest.raises Only Works When the Exception Escapes
There's an important distinction here. Suppose your function catches its own exception:
def extract_audio(...): try: ... except ffmpeg.Error: logger.error(...) return None
The exception never reaches the caller. Therefore, this won't work:
with pytest.raises(ffmpeg.Error): extract_audio(...)
There's nothing left for pytest.raises to catch. Instead, test the function's actual contract:
result = extract_audio(...)
assert result is None
And, if logging is part of the behavior you care about, use caplog to verify that the expected error was logged.
A useful rule of thumb:
If the function returns None from its except block, test the return value rather than expecting an exception.
 Parametrize: One Test, Many Inputs
Suppose you need to test several timestamp formats. You could write three tests:
def test_timestamp_one(): ...
def test_timestamp_two(): ...
def test_timestamp_three(): ...
But the test logic is identical. That's exactly what pytest.mark.parametrize is for:
@pytest.mark.parametrize( "timestamp,expected_seconds", [ ("00:00:01", 1.0), ("00:01:00", 60.0), ("01:00:00", 3600.0), ],)def test_validate_timestamp_parses_valid_formats( timestamp, expected_seconds,): assert validate_timestamp(timestamp) == pytest.approx(expected_seconds)
Think of it like a form letter: the first argument names the blanks to fill in (timestamp, expected_seconds), and the second argument is a stack of filled-in versions. pytest prints one out and runs the test for each one:
test_validate_timestamp_parses_valid_formats[00:00:01-1.0]test_validate_timestamp_parses_valid_formats[00:01:00-60.0]test_validate_timestamp_parses_valid_formats[01:00:00-3600.0]
Each case can pass or fail independently.
 Why independence matters
You could achieve something similar with a loop:
def test_timestamps(): for timestamp, expected in cases: assert validate_timestamp(timestamp) == expected
But there's a major difference: a normal loop stops at the first failure. With parametrization, pytest runs every case. So one test run tells you exactly which inputs are broken instead of merely telling you:
test_timestamps failed
 When should you use it?
The signal is simple:
If you're about to write several nearly identical test functions that differ only in their input values, consider parametrize.It works just as well for valid inputs as it does for malformed or invalid ones.
 Grouping Tests in a Class
pytest supports test classes:
class TestGetVideoMetadata: def test_returns_none_for_missing_file(self): assert get_video_metadata("missing.mp4") is None
 def test_has_audio_true_when_audio_stream_present(self): ...
But classes aren't mandatory. Use them when they provide something useful, such as:
shared setupfixtures scoped to the groupapplying a marker to multiple testsDon't use a class purely because it feels more organized. A well-named test file already provides plenty of organization.
 An important detail about test classes
Each test method gets a fresh instance of the class. So this:
class TestSomething: def test_one(self): self.value = 1
 def test_two(self): assert self.value == 1
is not valid. test_two doesn't receive the instance used by test_one. That's intentional — tests should be isolated from one another. Depending on mutable state from another test creates order-dependent and difficult-to-debug failures.
 Fixtures
Fixtures are one of pytest's most useful features. A fixture is a function that provides something a test needs — think of it like an ingredient a recipe asks for by name. You don't prep it inside the recipe itself; you just say "I need sample_video_path" and pytest hands it to you already made.
# tests/conftest.py
import pytestfrom pathlib import Path
@pytest.fixturedef sample_video_path() -> Path: return Path(__file__).parent / "fixtures" / "sample.mp4"
A test can then request it simply by putting the fixture name in its parameters:
# tests/core/test_video_inspector.py
def test_metadata_against_real_file(sample_video_path): result = get_video_metadata(str(sample_video_path))
 assert result is not None
pytest sees sample_video_path in the test signature, finds the fixture with that name, runs it, and passes the result to the test. No import is required.
 Why conftest.py Matters
conftest.py is automatically discovered by pytest. Fixtures defined there are available to test files in the same directory and its subdirectories — it works like a shared pantry that any test file in that part of the tree can pull from without asking for a delivery.
For example:
tests/├── conftest.py├── core/│ └── test_video_inspector.py└── api/ └── test_transcription.py
A fixture defined in tests/conftest.py is available to both tests/core/ and tests/api/.
You can also have a more specific conftest.py deeper in the tree:
tests/├── conftest.py└── core/ ├── conftest.py └── test_video_inspector.py
The deeper fixture configuration can then be used specifically by that subtree. A useful convention is: root conftest.py for shared fixtures, nested conftest.py files for fixtures that are genuinely local to a particular test area.
 Fixture Scope
Fixtures don't necessarily have to run for every test. You can control their lifetime:
@pytest.fixture(scope="function") # default@pytest.fixture(scope="module") # once per test file@pytest.fixture(scope="session") # once per entire test run
The default is scope="function", which means a fresh fixture is created for every test. Prefer the default unless there is a good reason to reuse the fixture.
A broader scope can make sense when setup is genuinely expensive and safe to share. For example, generating a synthetic sample video once per session may be much cheaper than generating it once for every test.
 Built-in Fixtures Worth Knowing
pytest provides several useful fixtures out of the box.
tmp_path
Provides a unique temporary directory for each test. Great for anything that needs to write files.
caplog
Captures logging output. Useful when you want to verify that something logged an error or warning.
capsys
Captures stdout and stderr. Useful for testing CLI output.
monkeypatch
Temporarily changes attributes, environment variables, dictionary entries, and other values. pytest automatically restores the changes after the test.
You can inspect available fixtures with:
uv run pytest --fixtures
tmp_path in Practice
Suppose you want to verify that audio extraction creates an actual file:
def test_extract_audio_writes_real_file( sample_video_path, tmp_path,): output_path = tmp_path / "output.wav"
 result = extract_audio( str(sample_video_path), str(output_path), )
 assert result == str(output_path) assert output_path.exists()
This is an integration-style test. It actually runs FFmpeg and checks that a real file was created. But because tmp_path is temporary, the test doesn't leave generated files scattered around your project — pytest creates the directory and handles its cleanup.
 Mocking: Two Tools, Different Jobs
Python gives you unittest.mock. pytest gives you monkeypatch. They overlap, but each one shines in a different situation.
unittest.mock.patch
Use patch when you want a more capable mock, particularly when you need to inspect how something was called.
from unittest.mock import patch
def test_metadata_no_audio(): fake_probe = { "format": { "filename": "silent.mp4", "duration": "10.0", }, "streams": [ { "codec_type": "video", "r_frame_rate": "25/1", }, ], }
 with patch( "clipper.core.video_inspector.ffmpeg.probe", return_value=fake_probe, ): result = get_video_metadata("silent.mp4")
 assert result["has_audio"] is False
patch temporarily replaces the target with a mock. It is particularly useful when you want to assert things like:
mock_input.assert_called_once_with("in.mp4")
monkeypatch
monkeypatch is pytest's own fixture. It's particularly convenient for simple temporary substitutions.
def test_uses_default_bitrate_env_var(monkeypatch): monkeypatch.setenv( "CLIPPER_DEFAULT_BITRATE", "256k", )
 assert get_default_bitrate() == "256k"
There's no context manager and no manual cleanup — pytest automatically restores the environment variable after the test. You can also replace attributes with monkeypatch.setattr(...) or dictionary entries with monkeypatch.setitem(...).
patch vs monkeypatch: A Practical Mental Model
Imagine your code is a toy robot and you want to test what happens when one of its components behaves differently. You don't want to actually break the component — you just want to temporarily pretend that it behaves differently.
monkeypatch is like putting a temporary sticky note over the component: "For this test, pretend this value is different." pytest removes the note when the test finishes.
patch is another version of the same idea, but with a much more powerful mock object behind it. patch can easily track call count, arguments, return values, exceptions, and chained calls.
Both clean themselves up reliably when used correctly. With patch, the common form in this project is:
with patch(...): ...
The mock is restored automatically when the block ends, even if the test fails.
 Which One Should You Use?
A practical rule:
NeedUseAssert how something was calledpatchCheck call count or exact argumentspatchMock a chained/fluent APIpatchReplace an environment variablemonkeypatchTemporarily change one attributemonkeypatch.setattr(...)Temporarily change a dictionary entrymonkeypatch.setitem(...)Replace an external dependency and inspect the mockpatchThe important thing isn't to memorize a strict rule. It's to recognize the distinction:
If you need to inspect how the dependency was used, patch is usually the natural choice. If you just need to temporarily replace a value or attribute, monkeypatch is often simpler.
side_effect: Make a Mock Fail
Mocks aren't only useful for returning fake successful results. They can also simulate failures.
return_value means "always return this." side_effect means "raise this exception instead."
with patch( "clipper.core.video_inspector.ffmpeg.probe", side_effect=ffmpeg.Error( cmd="ffprobe", stdout=b"", stderr=b"bad file", ),): result = get_video_metadata("bad.mp4")
This lets you exercise failure paths without needing to create a genuinely broken video file.
 Mock the Boundary, Not Your Own Logic
This is probably the most important mocking rule in the entire guide:
Mock the boundary, not the logic you're trying to test.Suppose your code does this:
probe = ffmpeg.probe(path)
The interesting logic is what your application does with the result. So mock ffmpeg.probe and provide realistic fake data — don't mock the parsing logic itself. A test that mocks everything, including the thing you're trying to test, can end up proving nothing more than: "my mocks returned what I told them to return."
Put another way — you're testing your recipe, not reinventing the oven. External boundaries are good mocking candidates:
FFmpegHTTP APIsdatabasesfilesystem operationscloud servicesexternal processesYour own business logic is usually what you want to execute for real.
 The Most Common Mocking Mistake: Patching the Wrong Path
This catches a lot of people. Suppose your module contains:
# video_inspector.py
import ffmpeg
def get_video_metadata(path): return ffmpeg.probe(path)
You might think you should patch ffmpeg.probe. But that's not necessarily the correct target — the code under test looks up ffmpeg in its own module namespace. Therefore, patch where the name is looked up:
patch( "clipper.core.video_inspector.ffmpeg.probe")
The general rule is:
Patch where the object is looked up, not where it was originally defined.If you patch the wrong path, the real dependency may still run. That can make a test unexpectedly hit FFmpeg, the network, a database, or some other external system.
 Mocking a Chained Call
Some APIs aren't a single function call. For example, ffmpeg-python can use a fluent chain:
ffmpeg.input(...).output(...).overwrite_output().run(...)
Mocking that requires walking the chain. MagicMock automatically creates mocks for attributes you access, so mock_input.return_value represents the result of ffmpeg.input(...), .output.return_value represents the next link in the chain, and so on until you reach .run — the actual operation you want to make fail.
def test_extract_audio_sad_path(caplog): fake_error = ffmpeg.Error( cmd="ffmpeg", stdout=b"", stderr=b"encoding failed", )
 with patch( "clipper.core.video_inspector.ffmpeg.input" ) as mock_input: mock_run = ( mock_input .return_value .output .return_value .overwrite_output .return_value .run ) mock_run.side_effect = fake_error
 result = extract_audio( "in.mp4", "out.wav", )
 assert result is None assert "error" in caplog.text.lower()
Walking the chain into its own variable (mock_run) before setting side_effect keeps the assignment itself simple and unambiguous — trying to set an attribute in the middle of a long parenthesized chain is a common source of syntax mistakes.
 Organizing Your Test Files
A simple and predictable test layout goes a long way. If your source looks like:
src/└── clipper/ └── core/ └── video_inspector.py
mirror it under tests/:
tests/└── core/ └── test_video_inspector.py
This makes it immediately obvious where the tests for a source module live.
 Keep tests/ Outside src/
Use:
project/├── src/├── tests/└── pyproject.toml
rather than:
src/├── clipper/└── tests/
Keeping tests outside the package helps avoid accidentally shipping them with your built distribution and keeps the distinction between application code and test code clear.
 You Usually Don't Need __init__.py
pytest doesn't require your test directories to be Python packages. So this is perfectly fine:
tests/├── core/│ └── test_video_inspector.py└── api/ └── test_transcription.py
No __init__.py required. There can be edge cases where you intentionally want package semantics, but don't add __init__.py to test directories just because you think pytest requires it. It doesn't.
 Keep Fixtures Separate from Test Code
tests/├── conftest.py├── fixtures/│ └── sample.mp4└── core/ └── test_video_inspector.py
This makes the distinction obvious: test_*.py contains test logic, fixtures/ contains test data.
 Mark Slow and External Tests
Not every test costs the same amount to run. A test that calls real FFmpeg is different from a test that checks a pure Python function.
You can mark integration tests:
@pytest.mark.integrationdef test_extract_audio_against_real_file(...): ...
Then register the marker in pyproject.toml:
[tool.pytest.ini_options]markers = [ "integration: calls real ffmpeg/ffprobe against a fixture file",]
Now you can run the fast suite without integration tests:
pytest -m "not integration"
And run everything with:
pytest
This gives you a useful distinction between fast unit tests and slower integration tests.
 Debugging pytest Without Sprinkling print() Everywhere
pytest captures output by default. That can be surprising when you're debugging — a print(result) that produces nothing on screen. Here are the options you'll reach for most often.
-s: Show stdout/stderr
uv run pytest -s
This disables output capturing, so your print() statements become visible. It's useful, although there are usually better debugging tools than adding prints everywhere.
-k: Run Tests by Name
If you're working on audio extraction, there's no reason to run 200 unrelated tests.
uv run pytest -k "extract_audio"
pytest runs tests whose names match the expression. This is one of the most useful options during active development.
-x: Stop at the First Failure
uv run pytest -x
Instead of getting a wall of failures, pytest stops after the first one. This is particularly useful when fixing a cascading failure.
--pdb: Drop Into the Debugger
uv run pytest --pdb
When a test fails, pytest drops you into an interactive debugger at the point of failure. Inside the debugger, you can inspect variables and control execution — c continues, q quits. This can be much faster than trying to predict where a bug is before running the test.
-vv: More Verbose Output
uv run pytest -vv
Useful when assertions involve large dictionaries, long strings, or parametrized tests and you want more detail in the output.
--lf: Run Only the Last Failures
uv run pytest --lf
--lf means "last failed." It reruns tests that failed during the previous run instead of running the entire suite. This is particularly useful when you're fixing several failures one by one.
 A Practical Debugging Command
These options can be combined:
uv run pytest -k "extract_audio" -x --pdb
This means: run only tests matching extract_audio, stop at the first failure, and open the debugger at the failure. That's a very practical development loop.
 Running a Specific Test
pytest doesn't natively use line numbers to select a test. This isn't standard pytest test selection:
pytest test_file.py:29
Instead, select by node ID:
pytest tests/core/test_video_inspector.py::test_metadata_no_audio
Or use -k:
pytest -k "metadata_no_audio"
Editors such as VS Code and PyCharm can provide "run this test" buttons. They translate your selection into pytest's name-based test selection behind the scenes. There are plugins that provide literal line-number selection, but you generally don't need one.
 Quickly Inspecting a Return Value
Sometimes you just want to see what a function actually returned. One quick technique is to deliberately make an assertion fail:
def test_scratch(sample_video_path): result = get_video_metadata(str(sample_video_path))
 assert result == {}
If {} isn't the actual result, pytest's failure output will show you the value. Delete the temporary test afterward.
Another option is:
uv run pytest --showlocals
or the shorthand -l, which shows local variables when a test fails.
 Dealing with Slow Tests
Don't guess which tests are slow. Measure them.
uv run pytest --durations=10
This reports the ten slowest tests after the run. You may discover that one or two tests account for most of the delay. Optimizing everything before measuring can waste the very time you're trying to save.
 Mark Slow Tests
Tests that load a real model or perform real inference are good candidates for a slow marker:
@pytest.mark.slowdef test_transcribe_real_audio_produces_valid_shape( sample_speech_path,): ...
Register the marker:
[tool.pytest.ini_options]markers = [ "integration: calls real ffmpeg/ffprobe against a fixture file", "slow: tests that load a real model or run real transcription",]
Then your normal development loop can skip them:
pytest -m "not slow"
And your complete suite can still run with pytest.
 Caching Can Already Solve Some Performance Problems
Suppose your application loads a model once at module level, and subsequent calls reuse it. Then only the first test that needs the model may pay the expensive loading cost — the others can reuse the already-loaded instance.
You can verify whether this is actually happening with uv run pytest --durations=10. If the first model-related test is slow and subsequent tests are much faster, your existing caching may already be doing the job. If every test is slow, something may be reloading the model when it shouldn't. Measure first.
 Parallelizing the Suite
If the entire suite is slow, rather than just a handful of expensive tests, parallel execution may help.
uv add --dev pytest-xdistuv run pytest -n auto
-n auto lets xdist determine a useful number of workers. But don't reach for parallelization automatically — for many projects, simply excluding slow tests during development (pytest -m "not slow") is enough.
 Coverage Is a Flashlight, Not a Scoreboard
Coverage is useful. It tells you which lines of code weren't exercised by your tests.
uv run pytest --cov=src
This can help you find code paths you haven't thought about. But coverage doesn't tell you whether your tests are good. You can achieve 100% coverage with tests that assert almost nothing meaningful:
def test_everything(): my_function()
The code executed. Coverage increases. But the test may tell you almost nothing about whether the behavior is correct. So treat coverage as a flashlight — use it to illuminate parts of the code you haven't tested. Don't treat it as a scoreboard you have to maximize.
 A Simple Checklist for Every New Test
When adding tests for a new function or feature, ask:
 1. What's the happy path?
What should happen when everything is valid?
 2. What's at least one edge case?
Consider: empty input, missing fields, boundary values, unexpected but valid combinations.
 3. What's the failure mode?
What should happen when input is invalid, an external dependency fails, a file doesn't exist, or an API returns an unexpected result?
 4. What should be mocked?
Usually mock things that are external, slow, non-deterministic, or side-effecting. But let your own logic run for real.
 5. Is the test asking one question?
If the test name contains the word "and," that's sometimes a sign that you're testing two behaviors at once. A test should ideally answer one clear question.
 The Mental Model I Ended Up With
pytest can look like a large collection of features when you're first learning it. But after working with it for a while, I found that most of what I actually needed came down to a few ideas.
Tests are ordinary Python functions. pytest discovers them through naming conventions.
Assertions are ordinary Python assert statements. pytest makes their failures informative.
Fixtures provide reusable things that tests need. conftest.py makes shared fixtures available without imports.
Parametrization lets you run the same test logic against multiple inputs.
Mocks let you replace boundaries you don't want to exercise for real. Things like FFmpeg, APIs, databases, and other external systems are often good candidates — while the logic you're actually testing should usually run normally.
Markers let you separate tests by purpose or cost. And the debugging tools make it much easier to figure out why something failed without resorting to print() everywhere.
Most importantly, I stopped thinking of testing as "how do I get my coverage number up?" and started thinking more in terms of "what question am I trying to answer with this test?" For me, that shift made pytest much easier to understand.
The syntax is the easy part.
